I write market reports for a living, and I want to tell you a secret about them. They are written with nouns. A rise in spending. The growth of demand. The reduction of manual work. Nouns sound serious, and they let you put a lot of information into one line. But nobody talks like that. When you take a number from my report into a sales call, turn the noun back into a verb. Do not say there was an increase in the adoption of automation. Say more companies are automating. It is shorter, and people remember it. The other thing I always tell salespeople is to read the method before the headline. Who answered the survey? How many respondents? Which segment? A growth rate of nine per cent means one thing for a market of two hundred companies and something very different for a market of twenty thousand.

When a vendor shows me a market report in the first meeting, I usually stop listening. I do not need to hear that the market is growing. I can read that myself. What I need is one number from the report that is about me. For example, last month a vendor told me that almost half of finance directors delay a purchase because of the connection with SAP. Then he asked me if that was true for us. It was. That one number started a twenty-minute conversation about our real problem. So my advice is simple. Bring one number, not twenty. Say it in plain words. And then ask a question about my company, not about the market.
